title: Time and std::chrono
summary: `<chrono>` models time with three ideas: **durations** (how long), **clocks** (where time comes from) and **time points** (a moment on a clock). The types make unit mistakes impossible. C++20 adds **calendar dates**, **time zones** and formatting.
markdown:
## Three building blocks ```mermaid flowchart LR C["Clock
system_clock: wall time
steady_clock: never adjusted"] -->|"now()"| TP["time_point
a moment"] TP -->|"tp2 - tp1"| D["duration
a length of time"] D -->|"tp + d"| TP ``` | Concept | Is | Example | |---|---|---| | **Duration** | A length of time, with its unit in the type | `1500ms` | | **Clock** | A source of the current time | `std::chrono::steady_clock` | | **Time point** | A specific moment, measured on one clock | The result of `now()` | The arithmetic is restricted to what makes sense: two time points subtract to a duration, a time point plus a duration is a time point, and two time points cannot be added. ## Durations ```cpp #include #include int main() { using namespace std::chrono_literals; const auto a{ 1500ms }; const auto b{ 2s }; const auto total{ a + b }; // 3500ms const auto whole{ std::chrono::duration_cast(total) }; // 3s const std::chrono::duration fractional{ total }; // 3.5 seconds std::cout << total.count() << ' ' << whole.count() << ' ' << fractional.count() << '\n'; return 0; } ``` `using namespace std::chrono_literals;` enables the suffixes. This is one of the few `using namespace` directives worth writing, and it belongs inside a function. | Literal | Type | |---|---| | `5h`, `5min`, `5s` | `hours`, `minutes`, `seconds` | | `5ms`, `5us`, `5ns` | `milliseconds`, `microseconds`, `nanoseconds` | | `std::chrono::days{ 3 }` | `days`; also `weeks`, `months`, `years` (C++20) | The unit is part of the type, so the compiler does the conversions and refuses the lossy ones. | Expression | Result | |---|---| | `2s + 500ms` | `2500ms`: converted to the finer unit automatically | | `std::chrono::seconds s{ 1500ms };` | Error: converting to a coarser unit loses information | | `duration_cast(1500ms)` | `1s`: an explicit, truncating conversion | | `duration d{ 1500ms };` | `1.5` seconds: a floating-point duration loses nothing | A whole class of bugs, "was that parameter in seconds or milliseconds?", cannot be written. ## Measuring elapsed time ```cpp const auto start{ std::chrono::steady_clock::now() }; doWork(); const auto end{ std::chrono::steady_clock::now() }; const auto elapsed{ std::chrono::duration_cast(end - start) }; std::println("Took {}", elapsed); // Took 42ms ``` | Clock | Represents | Can jump | Use for | |---|---|---|---| | `system_clock` | The calendar time of day | Yes: clock sync, a user changing the time | Timestamps, dates | | `steady_clock` | Time since an arbitrary start | Never | **Measuring intervals** | > [!tip] Always measure with `steady_clock` > A `system_clock` adjusted mid-measurement can produce a negative or wildly wrong duration. ## Sleeping ```cpp #include std::this_thread::sleep_for(500ms); std::this_thread::sleep_until(std::chrono::steady_clock::now() + 2s); ``` ### A fixed-rate loop ```cpp using Clock = std::chrono::steady_clock; constexpr auto tick{ 16ms }; // about 60 updates per second auto next{ Clock::now() }; while (running) { update(); render(); next += tick; std::this_thread::sleep_until(next); } ``` Sleeping **until** the next scheduled moment keeps the rate steady. Sleeping **for** 16 ms after each iteration would let the time taken by `update` and `render` accumulate as drift. ## Calendar and time zones C++20 added calendar types that read almost like the dates themselves. ```cpp #include #include int main() { using namespace std::chrono; const year_month_day today{ floor(system_clock::now()) }; std::println("{}", today); // for example 2026-11-12 const auto birthday{ 2000y / March / 14 }; std::println("{}", birthday.ok()); // true: it is a real date const auto endOfFebruary{ 2028y / February / last }; std::println("{}", endOfFebruary); // 2028/Feb/last: "the last day of February 2028" const sys_days first{ 2026y / January / 1 }; const sys_days christmas{ 2026y / December / 25 }; std::println("{} days", (christmas - first).count()); // 358 const weekday day{ sys_days{ 2026y / November / 11 } }; std::println("{}", day); // Wed return 0; } ``` | Type | Is | |---|---| | `year_month_day` | A calendar date as three fields. It can represent invalid dates; `ok()` checks. | | `sys_days` | A time point with a resolution of one day. Use it for arithmetic. | | `weekday` | A day of the week | | `zoned_time` | A time point paired with a time zone | ```cpp const zoned_time tokyo{ "Asia/Tokyo", system_clock::now() }; std::println("{:%Y-%m-%d %H:%M}", tokyo); ``` The `%` codes are the chrono format specifications ([[10.07 Formatting with stdformat and stdprint]]): `%Y` year, `%m` month, `%d` day, `%H` hour, `%M` minute, `%S` second. ## Check yourself ```quiz ? Which clock should you use to time code? - `std::chrono::system_clock` + `std::chrono::steady_clock` - `std::chrono::utc_clock` - Any of them; they are the same > `steady_clock` is monotonic and never adjusted. `system_clock` can jump when the computer's time is changed. ? Why does `std::chrono::seconds s{ 1500ms };` not compile? + Losing precision must be asked for with `duration_cast` - Because `ms` is not a valid suffix - Because durations cannot be initialized with braces - Because seconds can only hold whole minutes > 1500 ms is 1.5 seconds, which `seconds` cannot hold exactly. `std::chrono::duration_cast` truncates on request. ? What do you get by subtracting one time point from another? - A time point - A `double` number of seconds + A duration - A calendar date > Time point minus time point gives a duration. Time point plus duration gives another time point. ? Why use `sleep_until` in a fixed-rate loop? - Because `sleep_for` is not allowed in loops - To use less power - To make the loop run as fast as possible + It absorbs the time the work took, so the loop does not drift > With `sleep_for`, the work time adds to each period. `sleep_until(next)` keeps every tick on schedule. ```
ideas:
1. Write a stopwatch: press Enter to start, to record a lap and to stop. Show laps as `mm:ss.mmm`.
2. Write a countdown timer that prints the remaining seconds once a second.
3. Print how many days old you are and the weekday you were born on.

cards.q: Which clock should you use to time code?
cards.a:
`std::chrono::steady_clock`

`steady_clock` is monotonic and never adjusted. `system_clock` can jump when the computer's time is changed.

Losing precision must be asked for with `duration_cast`

1500 ms is 1.5 seconds, which `seconds` cannot hold exactly. `std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::seconds>` truncates on request.

cards.q: What do you get by subtracting one time point from another?
cards.a:
A duration

Time point minus time point gives a duration. Time point plus duration gives another time point.

cards.q: Why use `sleep_until` in a fixed-rate loop?
cards.a:
It absorbs the time the work took, so the loop does not drift

With `sleep_for`, the work time adds to each period. `sleep_until(next)` keeps every tick on schedule.
